question: Parents bring a 2-year-old girl to a general practitioner because they have noticed a 'white glow' in her right eye when light falls on it, particularly in photographs. She has no pain and her vision appears normal to parents. On torch examination, a white pupillary reflex is visible in the right eye. What is the SINGLE most important next step?

answers.text: Reassure the parents that this is likely a normal photographic red-eye artefact and review in 3 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect and potentially dangerous. Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Reassurance without urgent ophthalmology referral is the most common cause of catastrophic diagnostic delay.

answers.text: Prescribe glasses for possible refractive error as this may cause a white reflex in photographs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Leukocoria is NOT caused by refractive error. This response misidentifies the finding and dangerously delays the diagnosis of what may be retinoblastoma.

answers.text: Urgent (same-day) referral to an ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Leukocoria mandates urgent ophthalmology referral. Retinoblastoma is the commonest primary intraocular malignancy of childhood (mean age 18 months). Delayed diagnosis means enucleation instead of globe-salvage therapy, or worse — metastatic disease.

answers.text: Arrange MRI of the brain and orbits within the next 2 weeks as a non-urgent investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While MRI is an important investigation for retinoblastoma (to assess optic nerve involvement), it must be arranged by an ophthalmologist after urgent examination. Organising non-urgent imaging without immediate ophthalmology referral delays the diagnosis inappropriately.

overallFeedback.feedback: Every child with leukocoria needs urgent ophthalmology referral the same day. Retinoblastoma is the diagnosis to exclude first. Early diagnosis allows globe-salvage; late diagnosis may require enucleation or result in metastatic disease.
Excellent. Leukocoria in a child = retinoblastoma until proven otherwise = same-day ophthalmology referral. This is one of the most critical 'can't miss' diagnoses in paediatric medicine.
